stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about gauging stations?
stimulus: For decades, hydrologists have measured river discharge with gauging stations: permanent structures anchored to a riverbank that record water height around the clock. Building one can cost tens of thousands of dollars, so many small mountain streams have never been measured at all. Researchers in Nepal recently tested a cheaper approach. Volunteers filmed a stretch of stream with a phone, and software estimated flow speed from the movement of floating leaves and twigs. The estimates closely matched readings from a nearby station.
choices: They tend to give less accurate readings than phone-based estimates do.
Their high cost helps explain why many small streams have gone unmeasured.
They record water height during the day but not during the night.
They will soon be removed from rivers and replaced by volunteer videos.
explanation: The text says a station can cost tens of thousands of dollars and then uses 'so' to link that cost to the fact that many small streams have never been measured. Saying the cost helps explain the gap is exactly one step beyond what the text states.

A.why: You assumed the new method beat the old one. The text says the phone estimates closely matched the station's readings, so it never says the stations are less accurate.

C.why: You misread a detail. The text says stations record water height 'around the clock,' which includes the night.

D.why: You fell for the absolute claim. The text shows a cheaper method that works for unmeasured streams. It never says stations will be removed anywhere, let alone everywhere.

stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about the handwritten transcriptions made by early folk-song collectors?
stimulus: Early collectors of folk songs usually wrote melodies down by ear, turning what a singer performed into standard musical notation. Some collectors also brought wax-cylinder machines to the same sessions. When musicologist Hanna Lindqvist compared the transcriptions with these recordings, she found that collectors had often "corrected" notes that fell between the pitches of a piano keyboard. They had also smoothed irregular rhythms into tidy, regular measures.
choices: They were written down only after the collectors had replayed the wax cylinders.
They are of no value to musicologists who study folk songs today.
They may not show exactly how the singers actually performed the songs.
They kept irregular rhythms but altered pitches that fell between piano keys.
explanation: Lindqvist found that collectors changed both pitches and rhythms when they wrote songs down. The direct implication is that the written versions may differ from what the singers actually sang.

A.why: You invented the process. The text says collectors wrote melodies down by ear from the live performance. The recordings were used later, by Lindqvist, to check them.

B.why: You fell for the absolute claim. The text shows the transcriptions have a limitation, not that they are worthless.

D.why: You stopped reading halfway through. The pitch part is right, but the text says collectors also smoothed irregular rhythms, so they did not keep them.

stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about the leaf-edge method of estimating ancient temperatures?
stimulus: Paleobotanists often estimate the temperature of an ancient climate by finding the proportion of fossil leaves with smooth rather than toothed edges. The method rests on a pattern seen in living plants: smooth-edged leaves are more common in warm regions, and toothed leaves are more common in cool ones. However, a recent survey of modern forests found that trees growing along streams and lakeshores tend to have toothed leaves even where temperatures are warm.
choices: It could give misleading results for fossils of plants that grew near water.
It cannot provide a useful estimate of temperature for any ancient climate.
It assumes that toothed leaves are more common in warm regions than cool ones.
It works most reliably for fossils found along ancient streams and lakeshores.
explanation: After 'However,' the text says streamside trees have toothed leaves even in warm places. Under this method, toothed leaves suggest a cool climate, so fossils from plants that grew near water could make a warm climate look cooler than it was.

B.why: You fell for the absolute claim. The survey points to a problem with one kind of site, not a failure of the method everywhere.

C.why: You reversed the pattern. The method assumes smooth-edged leaves are more common in warm regions and toothed leaves in cool ones.

D.why: You reversed the implication. Streamside sites are exactly where the method is likely to be least reliable.

stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about breeding-bird surveys that rely on human observers?
stimulus: Most breeding-bird surveys rely on observers who walk a set route at dawn and note every species they see or hear. In a study in a Finnish wetland, researchers placed automatic sound recorders along the routes and left them running day and night. The recorders detected several secretive marsh birds, such as rails and bitterns, that observers had seldom reported. The researchers suggest this is likely because these species call mainly after dark.
choices: They detect rails and bitterns more often than automatic recorders do.
They miss every marsh bird species that lives in Finnish wetlands.
They are carried out mainly in wetlands rather than in forests or fields.
They may undercount bird species that call mostly during the night.
explanation: Observers walk their routes at dawn, and the birds they missed call mainly after dark. The implication is that dawn surveys may undercount night-calling species. That is one step beyond the text and no more.

A.why: You reversed the finding. The recorders picked up rails and bitterns that observers had seldom reported.

B.why: You fell for the absolute claim. The text names only a few secretive species, and observers 'seldom' reported them, which is not the same as never.

C.why: You treated one study's setting as the general rule. The text describes a single wetland study and says nothing about where most surveys take place.

stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about hand-timed sprint results?
stimulus: Coaches have long timed sprint races with handheld stopwatches. In a recent comparison, researchers timed the same 100-meter races both by hand and with electronic sensors triggered by the starting gun. The hand times averaged about 0.2 seconds faster. The researchers explain that timers tend to start their watches a split second after the gun fires. But they can watch the runner approach the finish line and stop the watch right on time.
choices: They are too inaccurate to be of any use to coaches who track sprinters.
They tend to be slightly slower than times recorded by electronic sensors.
They may make sprinters appear slightly faster than they actually ran.
They depend mostly on how quickly sprinters react to the starting gun.
explanation: Hand times came out about 0.2 seconds faster because timers start late but stop on time. A shorter recorded time makes a runner look faster than they really were.

A.why: You fell for the absolute claim. A gap of about 0.2 seconds is a limitation, and the text never says hand timing is useless.

B.why: You reversed the direction. The text says hand times averaged about 0.2 seconds faster, not slower.

D.why: You mixed up whose reaction matters. The text blames the timer's delay in starting the watch, not the sprinter's reaction to the gun.

stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about weather balloons?
stimulus: Forecasters have long measured conditions high in the atmosphere with weather balloons, which are launched twice a day. Each balloon records a single pass upward, so a storm that develops in the hours between launches may go unrecorded until the next one. Atmospheric scientist Lena Okafor is testing ground-based sensors that scan the air overhead every ten minutes.
choices: They provide no reliable measurements of conditions high in the atmosphere.
They can miss atmospheric changes that occur in the hours between launches.
They record conditions more often than Okafor's ground-based sensors do.
They cost more to operate than any network of ground-based sensors.
explanation: The text says each balloon records a single pass and that a storm forming between launches "may go unrecorded." Taking one step from that, you get that balloons can miss changes that happen between launches. That is the drawback Okafor's more frequent sensors are meant to fix.

A.why: You turned a limitation into a total failure. The text says balloons can miss changes between launches, not that their measurements can't be trusted at all. Forecasters have relied on them for a long time.

C.why: You reversed the comparison. Balloons go up twice a day and the sensors scan every ten minutes, so the sensors measure far more often.

D.why: The text never mentions cost. You brought in a common reason for replacing an old method that this passage doesn't give.

stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about Reyes's habit of studying his sketches for days?
stimulus: In woodcut printing, an artist carves away every part of a wooden block that should remain blank, leaving raised areas to carry the ink. Once wood has been cut away, it cannot be put back. Printmaker Tomas Reyes therefore draws each design in pencil directly on the block and studies it for several days before he makes a single cut.
choices: It lets him repair mistaken cuts before the block is ever inked.
It reveals that he values pencil drawing more than printmaking.
It helps him avoid making cuts that he could not later undo.
It ensures that none of his finished blocks ever contains an error.
explanation: The word "therefore" ties Reyes's careful study to the fact before it: wood that has been cut away cannot be put back. The one-step implication is that studying the sketch helps him avoid cuts he couldn't reverse.

A.why: The text says removed wood cannot be put back, so mistaken cuts can't be repaired. The careful study only matters because repair is impossible.

B.why: The pencil sketch is a step in making the print, not a rival to it. Nothing in the text compares how much Reyes values the two.

D.why: You took "helps avoid" and made it "guarantees." The text shows a careful habit, not a promise that he never makes a mistake.

stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about the bus lane on Harlow Avenue?
stimulus: City officials in Brennick credited a new bus lane on Harlow Avenue with shortening downtown commutes. However, a review by urban planner Aisha Morrow found that travel times had fallen by a similar amount on nearby streets without bus lanes. The drop came during the same months in which a large employer moved its offices out of downtown.
choices: It may not have been the main reason that commutes became shorter.
It had no effect at all on travel times along Harlow Avenue.
It made commutes longer on the streets near Harlow Avenue.
It should be removed so that the employer will return downtown.
explanation: "However" introduces the real finding. Commutes got shorter on streets without bus lanes too, and a large employer left during the same months. So something besides the lane may explain the change, and the lane may not deserve the credit officials gave it.

B.why: This is the subtype's trap: you turned "may not be the main reason" into "no effect at all." Morrow's review raises doubt about the officials' claim but doesn't prove the lane did nothing.

C.why: The text says travel times fell on the nearby streets. They did not get longer.

D.why: The text recommends nothing, and it never connects the employer's move to the bus lane. You went several steps past what the passage implies.

stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about asking people to recall what they ate?
stimulus: Nutrition researchers often ask study volunteers to list everything they ate the previous day. In a study led by Mei Tanaka, volunteers also photographed each meal and snack as they ate it. When the photographs were compared with the same volunteers' written lists, the photographs showed about 20 percent more snacks than the volunteers had recalled.
choices: It tends to cause people to overstate how many snacks they ate.
It produces records too inaccurate to be of any scientific use.
It is less common among researchers than photographing meals.
It may cause people to leave out some of the snacks they ate.
explanation: The photographs and the written lists covered the same eating, and the photographs showed more snacks. One step beyond that, people working from memory may leave out some of what they ate.

A.why: You got the direction backward. The lists showed fewer snacks than the photographs, so people understated their snacks.

B.why: This is the subtype's trap: a gap in one category of food doesn't make recall records useless. The text shows a limitation, not a total failure.

C.why: The text says researchers "often" use recall. Photographing meals appears only as an extra step in one study.

stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about the radar unit on the Velka River?
stimulus: Hydrologists have traditionally measured river flow by wading into the water with a current meter and taking readings at points across the channel. During floods, when flow data are most needed, that work becomes too dangerous to attempt. At a station on the Velka River, engineer Rafael Duarte has mounted a radar unit on a bridge to measure the water's surface speed from above.
choices: It can collect readings during floods, when wading would be unsafe.
It shows that current meters give inaccurate readings in any river.
It requires engineers to stand in the channel to take its readings.
It was installed mainly to protect the bridge from flood damage.
explanation: The text gives one drawback of the old method: wading is too dangerous during floods. The radar works from a bridge, above the water, so the one-step implication is that it can take readings when wading isn't safe.

B.why: This is the subtype's trap. The old method has a safety limit during floods, but the text never says current meters are inaccurate, let alone in every river.

C.why: The radar is mounted on a bridge and measures from above. That is the point of it, since standing in the channel is what becomes dangerous.

D.why: The bridge is only where the radar is mounted. The text says the radar measures water speed and gives no sign that it protects the bridge.
